Recent relevant work includes [Repeated Padding (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.06372), showing that padding strategy can materially affect GRU4Rec, and [RNN optimization analysis (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.21064), showing that long memory can increase parameter sensitivity even without exploding gradients. Neither establishes a validated diagnostic separating forgotten recent evidence, dominant older interactions, and last-item shortcuts. Gate interpretation requires implementation fidelity: in [PyTorch GRU](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/main/generated/torch.nn.GRU.html), hₜ=(1−zₜ)nₜ+zₜhₜ₋₁, so high z retains prior state. [Gating research](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.09890) explains how saturation can support retention while hindering gate learning.

Suggested diagnostic synthesis: within each trained category model, pair recent-item deletion/replacement with older-prefix deletion, holding the final item fixed; separately retain only the final item. Patch or reset the hidden state immediately before a recent suffix and replay that identical suffix. Compare target-score margins, ranks and HR@10 using identical candidates. Record reset/update-gate saturation, state-change norms, and target-margin gradients by history position; supplement gradients with [integrated gradients](https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.01365) and perturbations because low gradients alone do not establish irrelevance. Recent-input effects that disappear during subsequent updates suggest forgetting; prefix sensitivity despite a fixed suffix suggests older-state dependence; near-equivalent last-item-only predictions suggest a shortcut. These are hypotheses about model sensitivity, not causal user intent.

First verify left-padding invariance: padding steps must preserve state, and readout must select the final nonpadding index, never count−1. Run paired probes in evaluation mode with fixed validation users and candidates; stratify by history length and category. All interventions operate on the same checkpoint, without score fusion.
